verified.claim: c1: In Go 1.23, the range clause in a for-range loop accepts iterator functions of certain types as range expressions.
verified.evidence: The Go 1.23 release notes state that the range clause now accepts iterator functions as range expressions, which is the claim.

verified.claim: c2: The accepted iterator function types include func(yield func(V) bool) and func(yield func(K, V) bool).
verified.evidence: The range-functions blog says Seq and Seq2 are the iterator function types usable with for/range and defines them with exactly the two signatures named in the claim.

verified.claim: c3: The iter package defines Seq[V any] as func(yield func(V) bool).
verified.evidence: The blog's iter package definition gives Seq exactly as func(yield func(V) bool).

verified.claim: c4: The iter package defines Seq2[K, V any] as func(yield func(K, V) bool).
verified.evidence: The blog's iter package definition gives Seq2 exactly as func(yield func(K, V) bool).

verified.claim: c5: When a Seq is called as seq(yield), it calls yield(v) for each value v in the sequence.
verified.evidence: The iter package documentation for Seq states that seq(yield) calls yield(v) for each value in the sequence.

verified.claim: c6: When a Seq2 is called as seq(yield), it calls yield(k, v) for each pair (k, v) in the sequence.
verified.evidence: The iter package documentation defines Seq2 together with Seq as shorthands for iterators that pass 1 or 2 values per sequence element to yield; Seq2 is the two-value case, i.e. yield(k, v) per pair. (The Seq2-specific type paragraph is truncated in the supplied excerpt, but the general definition explicitly names Seq2.)

verified.claim: c7: A Seq stops early if yield returns false.
verified.evidence: The Seq documentation states that iteration stops early if yield returns false.

verified.claim: c8: A Seq2 stops early if yield returns false.
verified.evidence: The iter package defines iterators (Seq and Seq2 among them) as stopping when yield returns false; Seq2 is one of those defined iterators, so it stops early on a false return.

verified.claim: c9: The Go compiler translates a range-over-function loop into calls of the iterator function, passing the loop body as the yield function.
verified.evidence: Eli Bendersky says the compiler substitutes the yield function for the body of the original range loop, and the DoltHub article says the compiler converts the range loop into function calls; together these establish the claimed desugaring.

verified.claim: c10: A break or return in the loop body causes the yield function to return false, signaling the iterator to stop early.
verified.evidence: partial: The supplied material establishes only the break half: Eli Bendersky states that a break in the body is transformed into return false from the yield function. The material given does not state that a return in the loop body likewise makes yield return false, so the 'or return' part is not covered.

verified.claim: c11: If an iterator continues calling yield after yield has returned false, the program panics with the runtime error 'range function continued iteration after function for loop body returned false'.
verified.evidence: The DoltHub article's broken-iterator example shows the exact runtime panic message quoted in the claim.

verified.claim: c12: iter.Pull converts a push-style iterator sequence (Seq) into a pull-style iterator accessed by next and stop functions.
verified.evidence: The iter package documentation for Pull states it converts a push-style sequence into a pull-style iterator accessed by next and stop.

verified.claim: c13: iter.Pull2 converts a push-style Seq2 into a pull-style iterator accessed by next and stop functions.
verified.evidence: The iter package documentation for Pull2 states it converts the push-style iterator sequence into a pull-style iterator accessed by next and stop; Pull2 is the Seq2 variant of the function.

verified.claim: c14: Go 1.23 adds functions in the slices package that work with iterators.
verified.evidence: The range-functions blog states that new in Go 1.23 are functions in the slices package that work with iterators.

verified.claim: c15: Go 1.23 adds functions in the maps package that work with iterators.
verified.evidence: The same Go 1.23 blog statement covers the maps package functions that work with iterators; the release notes likewise list maps additions.

verified.claim: c16: Before Go 1.23, range-over-function could be tried in Go 1.22 by setting GOEXPERIMENT=rangefunc.
verified.evidence: The Ardan Labs article states that to try range-over functions in Go 1.22 one must set GOEXPERIMENT to rangefunc, matching the claim.

verified.claim: c17: A motivation for the range-over-function feature was that Go had no standard way to iterate over a sequence of values.
verified.evidence: The 2022 design discussion (rsc) opens with the statement that Go had no standard way to iterate over a sequence of values, which is the motivation the claim attributes to it.

verified.claim: c18: A secondary article states that range-over-function loops can perform as well as hand-written loops because the Go compiler can inline and optimize them, reducing overhead especially for simple cases.
verified.evidence: The claim is only that a secondary article states this performance claim; the Medium article states it in essentially the claimed terms, including inlining/optimizing and reduced overhead for simple cases.

inferences.reason: c1 and c2 establish that in Go 1.23 a for-range clause accepts iterator functions of the two named types; c3/c4 identify those types as iter.Seq/iter.Seq2; c5/c6 establish that calling seq(yield) invokes yield once per element (value, or key-value pair); and c9 establishes that the compiler translates the loop by calling the iterator function and substituting the loop body for yield. Together these premises justify the conclusion as stated.

c7 and c8 state that Seq/Seq2 stop early when yield returns false, and c10 states that break/return in the loop body makes yield return false, thereby signalling the iterator to stop. The two together support the conclusion that early stopping via break/return works this way.

c7/c8 say the sequence stops early when yield returns false, and c11 says that continuing to call yield after a false return panics with exactly that error. An iterator that keeps calling yield after false therefore cannot be correct, so a correct iterator must stop, and the stated panic is the consequence of not doing so.

c3/c4 establish that the iter package defines the standard iterator types Seq and Seq2; c12/c13 establish that iter.Pull and iter.Pull2 convert push-style sequences into pull-style iterators accessed via next and stop. This is exactly the conclusion.
c14 states Go 1.23 adds iterator-working functions in the slices package and c15 states the same for the maps package; jointly they support the conclusion.

c17 supplies the motivation (no standard way to iterate over a sequence of values) and c16 supplies the experimental availability in Go 1.22 via GOEXPERIMENT=rangefunc before the 1.23 release. Both conjuncts of the conclusion are covered.

c18 only establishes that a secondary article makes the performance claim; the conclusion's second conjunct ('the official documentation retrieved does not establish that performance equivalence') is a claim about the official documentation that c18 says nothing about. A premise about what the official docs do or do not establish is missing, so the conclusion does not follow from its listed premise.

The conclusion is the conjunction of its two named premises, c7 (a Seq stops early if yield returns false) and c8 (a Seq2 stops early if yield returns false), both within the same scope (Go 1.23 iter package). Assuming both premises true, the combined statement holds under exactly that scope; no additional premise is needed.

The conclusion restates premise c18 (that a secondary article states range-over-function loops can perform as well as hand-written loops because the compiler can inline and optimize them, reducing overhead especially for simple cases), including the attribution to a secondary article. Assuming c18 true, the attributed-position statement follows.
